translate_en|mods/Project Russia/common/: Chernozemsk. Author - RomaPozitiv <LINE> <LINE>Chernozemsk is a small urban-type settlement, lost amid vast plains and wheat fields. The name speaks for itself: the soil here is fertile—black, soft, and rich—and everything around seems to have grown from it—houses, roads, trees, people. In peacetime, the settlement lived at a leisurely pace, leaning toward agriculture and local production, yet it had its own character and even a certain coziness. <LINE> <LINE> The central part of Chernozemsk is organized around a large market—the bustling, long-standing heart of the settlement, where everything was sold: from potatoes to old radios. The market is a labyrinth of kiosks, pavilions, warehouses, and old trucks converted into stalls. In peacetime, it was crowded here, smelling of grilled meat, spices, and fresh bread. Now, however, the market is empty, ransacked, littered with overturned stalls—but it is precisely here that one can find leftover supplies, warm clothing, tools, and random resources that someone didn’t have time to take. <LINE> <LINE> A couple of blocks from the market lies Chernozemsk University. It’s not a major university, but a local one—agricultural or technical, with departments that taught farming, machinery, and rural economics. Student dorms, academic buildings, laboratories—all of this lies silent now, but the university building stands out for its scale and relative sturdiness. Here you can find equipment, books, and storage areas. Beyond the university, streets lined with village houses begin: well-kept, with carved shutters and grapevines along the fences, interspersed with long-abandoned log cabins where only empty beds and children’s toys remain on the floor. Here and there, wheat fields stretch between the houses—flat, open, and swept by the wind. Once, combine harvesters hummed here and grain-filled trailers rumbled. Now—only the rustle of grass and movement among the stalks, not always caused by the wind. On the outskirts of Chernozemsk—old collective farm buildings. Barns, garages, vegetable storage sheds, workshops. Inside them—tools, machinery, sometimes fuel. All of it is rusting, but it can still work. Gravel roads wind between them, leading to the fields and neighboring farmsteads. <LINE> <LINE> And, of course, the brewery holds a special place—the pride of the village. Huge, with metal tanks, a fragrant past, and the concrete silence of the present. Its buildings are clearly visible from any hill, and in this empty landscape, it looks like a fortress where no one brews beer anymore—only the muffled echo of footsteps from the dead inside can be heard. <LINE> <LINE> Chernozemsk doesn’t shout about itself. It stands among the fields, as if forgotten, yet already dead. It’s a place where the past hasn’t yet faded away, and the present—dangerous, murky—only draws you in. Here you can hide, find the remnants of civilization and supplies, and, of course, enjoy a tasty meal of vegetables from the garden.
Chernozyomsk, Tver region

Dmitrov. Author: I_ALT_I <LINE> <LINE> Dmitrov is an ancient town in the northern Moscow Region, nestled among hills, river valleys, and wooded edges. Its history dates back to the 12th century, and this is evident in everything: in the cobblestone streets, in the winding old neighborhoods, and in the majestic yet slightly lopsided silhouette of the cathedral on the hill. Everything here is compact but not cramped—the city lives at a measured pace, nestled among nature, as if slightly removed from the flow of time. <LINE> <LINE> The central part of Dmitrov stretches along the canals and the railway connecting it to Moscow and the northern regions. The historic center sets the main rhythm—with the Kremlin, domes, and narrow streets where shops alternate with old houses, and everything is imbued with a sense of a “living past.” Now these streets are silent, but once they were bustling with life: tourists, local grandmothers with berries, young men at the stalls. Now these places are filled with abandoned shops, silence, and the occasional footsteps—not always human. <LINE> <LINE> On the outskirts are more modern neighborhoods. Small five-story buildings, schools, shops, rows of garages. The private sector gives way to rural development: vegetable gardens, wooden houses, fences with peeling paint. Everything here seems to have failed to keep up with the changes—frozen in the transition from the old to the new. This is especially noticeable in the industrial zones on the outskirts—former warehouses, repair shops, service stations. They are now abandoned, but inside—there are still remnants of machinery, tools, spare parts, and fuel. <LINE> <LINE> Being a distance from Moscow, Dmitrov found itself on the sidelines of the initial waves of infection, so the city retained its supplies, suffered less destruction, and has a functioning infrastructure. The variety of building types offers freedom of choice—settle into a high-rise, retreat to a private home, or occupy a small warehouse on the outskirts. Vast forests, the Yakhroma River, and proximity to canals provide water, game, and timber. An excellent place to establish a sustainable base. The presence of factories and warehouses offers a chance to find rare tools, generators, building materials, and even vehicles. But the historic center, commercial districts, and the train station could have become gathering places for refugees, turning them into hotspots for infection. <LINE> <LINE> Now Dmitrov is a ghost town, where every alleyway holds traces of its former life. Here, you can still find supplies, working vehicles, and abandoned stations. But zombies are no rarity here either—especially in the shadows of the monastery walls or behind bus stops where people once waited for a bus to the region. It’s easy to get lost in this city. But it’s also easier here than anywhere else to go unnoticed.
Dmitrov, Moscow region

Dolgoprudny. Author: I_ALT_I <LINE> <LINE> Located just 4 km north of Moscow, the town of Dolgoprudny is not so big but strategically important suburb with a population of about 70,000 people prior to the zombie apocalypse. Thanks to its proximity to the capital and convenient transportation links, the city features residential neighborhoods as well as industrial, educational, and logistical infrastructure useful to survivors. However, due to its location, the city was quickly infected and was unable to mount any defense against the invasion. <LINE> <LINE> Founded as an airship manufacturing plant in the early 20th century, it gradually grew into a settlement called Direzhablstroy, and in the 1950s became a full-fledged city focused primarily on industrial activity, with numerous machine-building, chemical, and military plants constructed in the south. You can also visit the famous Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology (MIPT) here. <LINE> <LINE> At the time of the country’s economic collapse, control of the city fell into the hands of the Dolgoprudny organized crime group.
Dolgoprudny, Moscow region

Gorki. By MineLife <LINE> <LINE> The resort village of Gorki, with a population of about 3,000, is a typical example of an early 1990s suburban resort area—a combination of natural seclusion and Soviet-era infrastructure, some of which had already begun to fall into disrepair by 1993. Families came here on vacation packages, factory workers on company assignments, and those seeking peace and quiet away from the city. Gorki is surrounded by forests, with access to the water and dirt roads leading to dacha settlements and sanatoriums built back in the Soviet era. <LINE> <LINE> Today, this place is already feeling the effects of the collapse of the USSR: service has gradually deteriorated, parts of the buildings stand empty, and security and technical staff have been cut back. Nevertheless, the infrastructure remained intact: dormitories, administrative buildings, dining halls, warehouses, garages, and small outbuildings. The vacation homes were scattered across the grounds, surrounded by mixed forest, which created a sense of seclusion, but at the same time—isolation. <LINE> <LINE>
Gorki, Moscow region

Ivanovsky. Author: MineLife <LINE> <LINE> A small village in the Moscow Region with a population of about 2,000, located in a forested area away from major transportation routes. Before the apocalypse, it was a quiet, secluded place, consisting mainly of private homes and a sparse number of multi-story residential buildings. Now, it is a potentially ideal place for survivors who value autonomy and peace. <LINE> <LINE> The settlement consists mainly of private homes, fenced-in lots, and narrow streets, making it difficult for quick raids but excellent for establishing a long-term base. Thanks to its compact size and the surrounding forests, Ivanovsky remains an inconspicuous and relatively uncontaminated place—at least at first glance.
Ivanovskiy, Moscow region

Klin. Author: UKG <LINE> <LINE> Klin is a city near Moscow with a population of 94,000, located between Moscow and Tver on an ancient trade route. It lies on the banks of the Sestra River, which divides it into several irregular sections. A medium-sized city with an industrial past, residential neighborhoods, private housing, and green spaces tucked away among factories, roads, and old architecture. <LINE> <LINE> Despite its relative proximity to Moscow, Klin has always retained the characteristics of an independent, somewhat insular town. The center—with its wide streets, Soviet-era buildings, cultural centers, and remnants of merchant-era architecture—gradually gives way to prefabricated housing districts, then to industrial zones and residential outskirts. On the city’s outskirts lie villages, summer cottages, abandoned warehouses, vacant lots, and forest strips. <LINE> <LINE> Closer to the river, it is quieter. The old part of the city, with its green streets, fences, wooden houses, and empty courtyards, may seem peaceful, almost abandoned. In some places, there are overgrown lots, unfinished houses, and empty sheds. Here, you feel a sense of space and fresh air, but at the same time, a sense of helplessness. The Sestra River, winding its way through the entire city, divides the districts and can serve as a natural boundary or an obstacle, depending on the situation. On the outskirts—summer cottage communities, forests, dirt roads, and empty fields. These places were once bustling in the summer, full of people, barbecues, cars, and radios. Now they are empty, overgrown with grass, concealing both silence and danger. Here you can find remnants of civilization, but they are intertwined with oblivion.
Klin, Moscow region

Nazarovo. Authors: ZUBLUDOK, I_ALT_I <LINE> <LINE> Nazarovo is a small town located on the Volga River. Its approximate population is 62,000. During the Soviet era, from which it traces its roots, the city flourished and grew into what we have today. Nazarovo was founded in the 1960s, and due to its rapid growth, it quickly became a coveted destination for wealthy officials who dreamed of acquiring real estate in a promising mid-sized city. Then, in the 1980s, along with the country’s economic decline, the once-promising city began to ruin its reputation, turning into yet another godforsaken place teeming with scum and gangsters. Naturally, the former elite had long since moved out of Nazarovo, seeking more attractive locations in the region. <LINE> <LINE> Following the virus outbreak, it is clear that Nazarovo could become a vital hub for survivors due to its size, available resources, and proximity to other cities.
Nazarovo, Tver region

Rostov. Authors: YesDaddy, MineLife, Fenix, I_ALT_I, sergei, ReTurN  <LINE> <LINE> Rostov is one of Russia’s oldest cities, with a population of approximately 36,000, situated on the shores of Lake Nero and surrounded by plains, marshy outskirts, and dense forests. The city seems to have been carved out of another era: cobblestone streets, white-stone monastery walls, low-rise houses, and spacious courtyards create a sense of tranquility and detachment from time. Despite its relatively small size, Rostov has a complex structure: the old center with its architectural landmarks smoothly transitions into more chaotic residential development, then into the private sector and villages, gradually dissolving into the countryside. <LINE> <LINE> In peacetime, the city lived a leisurely provincial life. There were no major industrial zones or significant military presence here—everything revolved around trade, tourism, seasonal fishing, and agriculture. Shops, workshops, schools, and the hospital were located compactly, within walking distance, but the infrastructure was ill-equipped to handle major crises. Beyond the city center lies silence, with cars passing by rarely and houses standing empty, many of which have already begun to crumble from the ravages of time and moisture. <LINE> <LINE> The central part of the city, with its stone buildings and high walls, could potentially serve a defensive function. The monastery’s thick walls and its adjoining outbuildings are well-preserved and stand out against the backdrop of the fragile wooden structures scattered along the outskirts. However, the dense development around the lake, interwoven with narrow alleys and old courtyards, makes movement difficult and creates a sense of confinement. Any movement here can be heard from afar, especially in the silence of the abandoned city. <LINE> <LINE> Rostov is a place where the old is closely intertwined with nature and time. Amid the catastrophe, it became not the epicenter of chaos, but a quiet backwater: beautiful, majestic, and dangerous in its detachment.
Rostov, Yaroslavl region

Skhodnya. Author: I_ALT_I <LINE> <LINE> Skhodnya is a small town near Moscow, nestled in lush greenery; it is an independent town near Khimki with a population of 19,000. Nestled among hills, ravines, and deciduous forests, it has developed from the very beginning as a settlement with a scattered layout: here, old dachas, private homes, Soviet five-story apartment buildings, and low-rise residential buildings from later developments are all intermingled. The terrain is rugged, with steep slopes, shady trails, and steep ravines that divide the area into sections not always directly connected to one another. <LINE> <LINE> A railway runs through Skhodnya—a major artery that has shaped the character of its layout. It separates the central part, with its shops, schools, and older infrastructure, from the more remote outskirts, where the landscape transitions into gardens, cottages, and wooded summer cottage communities. This layout makes Skhodnya appear visually dense yet multi-layered. <LINE> <LINE> On the southern side of the city lies a zone of former industrial sites: here you’ll find a furniture factory, warehouses, and numerous stores selling furniture and home goods. Even after the decline of manufacturing began, this part of Skhodnya remained saturated with goods—tables, sofas, hardware, and finishing materials. These places, surrounded by concrete walls and dead-end passageways, look today like industrial ghosts—huge buildings that hummed during the day and stood empty at night. But within them, one can still find remnants of a past life—tools, materials, textiles, and sometimes supplies left behind in a hurry. <LINE> <LINE> Skhodnya itself, despite its proximity to Moscow, has always been a world apart. There was no city noise here, but neither was there any real rural simplicity. Life in the area moved slowly, unhurried, with a sense that everything was on the border—between the city and the forest, between noise and silence. Now that the familiar order has vanished, Skhodnya looks like a forgotten corner on the edge of a big city: hidden, overgrown with greenery, with many secluded spots and traces of its former life. It doesn’t stand out, but that is precisely what defines its character.
Skhodnya, Moscow region

Sloboda. Authors: Huel, MineLife <LINE> <LINE> Sloboda is a quiet village in the Klin urban district, nestled among wooded areas, fields, and the winding lanes of old country roads. Here, remnants of the Soviet way of life, industrial infrastructure, and the old, almost vanishing simplicity of village life intertwine. <LINE> <LINE> The central part of Sloboda is developed—here you can find paved streets, low-rise buildings, well-kept courtyards, small shops, and several large facilities that shaped local life before the disaster. One such place was the Zarechye House of Culture—a building with columns and a sloping roof where concerts, film screenings, gatherings, meetings with veterans, and simply dances for young people were held. Now it looks abandoned, but inside, the stage, the prop storage, chairs, and even forgotten posters have been preserved. This place is like a frozen cultural landmark against the backdrop of a crumbling world. <LINE> <LINE> Not far from the center was the Sloboda Sports and Recreation Center—a sports complex built under a regional development program, with gyms, a fitness center, showers, and outdoor sports fields. On the eastern side of the village stood a manufacturing plant—Apparaturschik, a factory that produced and repaired electrical equipment, control panels, power supplies, and other industrial components. <LINE> <LINE> All around were village houses, gardens, vegetable patches, fences, old swings, sheds, and creaking gates. Sloboda is a place where city life coexists with rural tranquility, and the air was always filled with a mixture of smoke, grass, and metal. Now a different kind of silence reigns here—one that is wary and heavy. People are almost nowhere to be seen, but traces of their recent presence are everywhere.
Sloboda, Moscow region

Uspensk. By UKG <LINE> <LINE> Uspensk is a city with character. Standing on the banks of a great river, it seems to have grown out of the water itself: stone embankments, wide bridges, riverside warehouses, and port cranes form its backbone, while the neighborhoods spread across the hills make up its body. Founded in ancient times, Uspensk has inherited from the past a merchant spirit, the domes of ancient churches, and a penchant for a leisurely, unhurried life. <LINE> <LINE> The city center is built on two levels: above—the old town with narrow streets, sloping roofs, pre-revolutionary buildings, and the ringing of bells; below, by the water—the port area, where everything is steeped in the scent of fuel oil, fish, and old wood. Once upon a time, cargo was unloaded here, carts clattered, and barges anchored in the roadstead. Now—silence. Only the wind rustles among the pallets, and the water lazily laps against the concrete of the pier. The Volga River flows through the entire length of Uspensk, slowly and majestically dividing the city into two parts. Bridges connect the banks, and along the water are fishing piers, boat stations, and abandoned motorboats. The cargo port itself—massive, with crane towers, iron staircases, and a labyrinth of containers—now looks like an industrial monument. Once, it fed the city. Now it has become its skeleton. <LINE> <LINE> To the east of the city stands a hydroelectric power plant. Its concrete spans, massive turbines, and echoing machine rooms once supplied the entire region with light. The plant is a world of its own: concrete-encased, protected, complex. Even in silence, it commands respect—as if it were still operating, though the lights have long since gone out. The train station is one of Uspensk’s key landmarks. It connected the city to the outside world, receiving trains from Moscow, the south, and the hinterlands. The train cars still stand here, empty, silent, with broken windows. Nearby is the market: covered pavilions, rows of containers, tents, stalls selling clothes, meat, vegetables, and appliances. Shops line the streets around the station: hardware stores, grocery stores, pharmacies, repair shops. It used to be a lively, bustling place where all segments of the city’s population intersected. Now, there are scattered remnants of what was once everyday life. <LINE> <LINE> Uspensk is a city where the old and the new have always coexisted side by side. Monasteries and prefabricated high-rises, wooden shops and concrete terminals, schoolyards and apartment entrances with 1970s mosaics. Everything here is steeped in history and routine, which is why it is especially painful to see how it has come to a standstill. Now the city is dead, but not abandoned. Shadows roam within the walls of the old center. Footsteps can be heard along the embankment. By the railroad tracks, something shuffles between the rails. Uspensk hasn’t given up—it has frozen, watching to see who will be the next to walk its streets.
Uspensk, Tver region
